title: Can, could, be able to and be allowed to

sections.title: Can, could and be able to: ability
sections.content:
We sometimes use be able to instead of can and could to talk about ability. We avoid be able to –
☆ when we talk about something that is happening as we speak:
• Watch me, Mum; I can stand on one leg. (not … I'm able to stand on one leg.)
☆ before passives:
• Films can now easily be streamed online. (rather than Films are now easily able to be streamed …)
☆ when the meaning is 'know how to':
• Can you cook? (rather than Are you able to cook?)

sections.title: Be able to vs could for single achievements
sections.content:
If we talk about a single achievement, rather than a general ability in the past, we usually use be able to rather than could. Compare:
• She swam strongly and was able to cross the river easily, even though it was swollen by the heavy rain. (not She swam strongly and could cross …; a single achievement)
• Sophie could play the flute quite well. (or … was able to …; a general ability)
However, it is usually more natural to use be able to –
☆ in negative sentences:
• I tried to get up but I couldn't move.
☆ with verbs of the senses, e.g. feel, hear, see, smell, taste, and with verbs of 'thinking', e.g. believe, decide, remember, understand:
• I could remember the crash, but nothing after that.
☆ after the phrases the only thing / place / time, and after all when it means 'the only thing':
• All we could see were his feet.
☆ to suggest that something almost didn't happen, particularly with almost, hardly, just, nearly:
• I could nearly touch the ceiling.

sections.title: Can and could: possibility
sections.content:
To talk about the theoretical possibility of something happening we use could, not can. However, we use can, not could, to say that something is possible and actually happens. Compare:
• It could be expensive to keep a cat. (= if we had one, it's possible that it would be expensive) and
• It can be expensive to keep a cat. (= people find it sometimes is)
We use can't, not couldn't, to say that something is theoretically or actually impossible:
• There can't be many people in the world who haven't watched television.
• The doctor can't see you this morning; he's busy at the hospital.

sections.title: Can/could for future possibility
sections.content:
We use can to indicate that there is a very real possibility of a future event happening. Using could suggests that something is less likely or that there is some doubt about it. Compare:
• We can stay with Jake in Oslo. (= we will be able to stay) and
• We could stay with Jake in Oslo. (= it's possible; if he's there)

sections.title: Could and be allowed to: permission
sections.content:
To say that in the past someone had general permission to do something – that is, to do it at any time – we can use either could or was / were allowed to. However, to talk about permission for one particular past action, we use was / were allowed to, but not could. Compare:
• Anyone was allowed to fish in the lake when the council owned it. (or … could fish …) and
• Although he didn't have a ticket, Ned was allowed to come in. (not … could come in.)
In negative sentences, we can use either couldn't or wasn't / weren't allowed to to say that permission was not given in general or particular situations:
• I couldn't / wasn't allowed to open the present until my birthday.

exercises.question: Valuables can / are able to be left in the hotel safe.
options: can (before passives, use can not be able to)
exercises.hint: Avoid 'be able to' before passives → use 'can'.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: can (before passives, use can not be able to)
In passive sentences, use can be + past participle. Are able to be is grammatically possible but very unnatural — English strongly prefers can be in passive constructions with ability/possibility meaning.

exercises.question: We could / were able to finish the hockey match before it started snowing too heavily.
exercises.hint: Single achievement (they finished the specific match) → were able to.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: were able to (single achievement)
Single achievement (they finished the specific match) → were able to.

exercises.question: The rebels could / were able to draw on the support of over 20,000 soldiers.
acceptable: Both could and were able to are possible (general situation)
exercises.hint: General ability/situation, not single achievement → both are possible.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: Both could and were able to are possible (general situation)
General ability/situation, not single achievement → both are possible.

exercises.question: Could you / Were you able to understand Professor Larsen's lecture? I found it really difficult.
acceptable: Both could you and were you able to are possible
exercises.hint: Verb of thinking/understanding — both forms are possible.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: Both could you and were you able to are possible
Verb of thinking/understanding — both forms are possible.

exercises.question: B: Sorry, I can't / I'm not able to play chess.
options: I can't (more natural — know how to)
exercises.hint: When meaning is 'know how to', use can/can't, not be able to.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: I can't (more natural — know how to)
When meaning is 'know how to', use can/can't, not be able to.

exercises.question: When the firefighters arrived they could / were able to put out the flames in a couple of minutes.
exercises.hint: Single achievement (putting out the specific fire) → were able to.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: were able to (single achievement)
Single achievement (putting out the specific fire) → were able to.

exercises.question: The air was so polluted in the city centre, I could hardly / was hardly able to breathe.
exercises.hint: With 'hardly' → use 'could' (more natural).
exercises.explanation:
Answer: could hardly (more natural — 'hardly' → use could)
With 'hardly' → use 'could' (more natural).

exercises.question: I know Petra had been decorating. I could / was able to smell the paint when I came in.
options: could (verb of sense, smell → use could)
exercises.hint: Verb of sense (smell) → use could, not was able to.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: could (verb of sense, smell → use could)
Verb of sense (smell) → use could, not was able to.

exercises.question: Can you / Are you able to drive without your glasses?
options: Can you (know how to = can, not be able to)
exercises.hint: When meaning is 'know how to', use can not be able to.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: Can you (know how to = can, not be able to)
Both can and are able to work here, but can is far more natural in everyday conversation when asking about ability. Are you able to sounds unnecessarily formal for this direct personal question.

exercises.question: No changes can / are able to be made to this rail ticket after purchase.
options: can be made (passive → use 'can', not 'be able to')
exercises.hint: Before passives, use 'can' not 'be able to'.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: can be made (passive → use 'can', not 'be able to')
In passive sentences with a negative subject (no changes), use can be made. The form are able to be made is grammatically awkward in English — passive + be able to is always replaced by can in natural usage.

exercises.question: He could / was able to untie the ropes without the guards noticing.
exercises.hint: Single achievement → was able to.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: was able to (single achievement)
Single achievement → was able to.

exercises.question: She looked all over the house, but couldn't / wasn't able to find her keys anywhere.
acceptable: Both couldn't and wasn't able to are possible
exercises.hint: Negative sentence — both couldn't and wasn't able to are natural.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: Both couldn't and wasn't able to are possible
Negative sentence — both couldn't and wasn't able to are natural.

exercises.question: I was very busy at work, but I could / was able to have a couple of days off last week.
exercises.hint: Particular occasion, not general permission → was able to.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: was able to (single specific occasion)
Particular occasion, not general permission → was able to.

exercises.question: We went camping … the day we arrived it ___ rain a lot on the coast.
exercises.hint: Theoretical possibility (sometimes rains a lot) → could.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: could
Theoretical possibility (sometimes rains a lot) → could.

exercises.question: We ___ believe how heavy the rain was.
exercises.hint: Negative: unable to believe → couldn't.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: couldn't
Use 'couldn't' for inability in the past or for an emphatic expression of disbelief. 'Can't' in the present, 'couldn't' in the past. 'Wasn't able to' is more formal but both are correct for past inability.

exercises.question: 'This tent ___ be assembled in two minutes with no previous experience.'
exercises.hint: Actual capability (it does happen) → can.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: can
'Can' expresses general capability or the theoretical possibility that something actually happens. Use 'can' when you're describing something that is genuinely achievable or does actually occur.

exercises.question: Now, there ___ be many people who haven't had difficulty.
exercises.hint: Theoretical possibility (imagining) → could.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: could
'Could' expresses a theoretical possibility — imagining what might be the case, or a hypothetical scenario. 'Can' describes actual or general capability; 'could' is more tentative and hypothetical.

exercises.question: A man came along and said that we ___ camp there — it was private property.
exercises.hint: Particular occasion, no permission given → weren't allowed to.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: weren't allowed to
Particular occasion, no permission given → weren't allowed to.

exercises.question: Well, we ___ stay here all night.
exercises.hint: Negative permission/ability in the past → couldn't.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: couldn't
Negative permission/ability in the past → couldn't.

exercises.question: They were very kind and we ___ camp at the end of their garden!
exercises.hint: Particular permission given on that specific occasion → were allowed to.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: were allowed to
Particular permission given on that specific occasion → were allowed to.

exercises.question: Sports coaches ___ be strict.
exercises.hint: General truth about possibility → can.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: can
'Can' expresses a general truth about what is possible or what sometimes happens. This is not ability in the individual sense but a statement about what occurs in general — similar to 'it is possible for'.

exercises.question: Lance ___ stay up later than nine.
exercises.hint: General restriction/rule → wasn't allowed to.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: wasn't allowed to
General restriction/rule → wasn't allowed to.

exercises.question: On his birthday he ___ watch television until ten.
exercises.hint: Special permission on a particular occasion → was allowed to.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: was allowed to
Special permission on a particular occasion → was allowed to.

exercises.question: All Lance ___ think of was going out with his friends.
exercises.hint: After 'all' meaning 'the only thing' → could.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: could
In the construction 'all + subject + could do', 'could' is fixed. It expresses the only option available — 'the only thing they were able to do'. This is a set pattern with 'could', not 'can'.

exercises.question: He ___ hardly wait for the Games to finish.
exercises.hint: With 'hardly' → use 'could'.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: could
'Hardly' belongs to a group of negative-meaning adverbs (barely, scarcely, rarely) that require 'could', not 'can'. Use: 'could hardly wait', 'could scarcely believe', 'could barely move'.

exercises.question: He ___ lose!
exercises.hint: Present impossibility (deduction about now) → can't.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: can't
Present impossibility (deduction about now) → can't.

exercises.question: His coach ___ celebrate — staying up until 11 o'clock!
exercises.hint: Particular permission given on a specific occasion → was allowed to.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: was allowed to
Particular permission given on a specific occasion → was allowed to.

exercises.question: She trained for years, and now she ___ (speak) five languages fluently.
exercises.hint: Present ability acquired over time → can or be able to.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: can speak
'Can' expresses present ability. 'Be able to' is also correct and slightly more formal, often used when emphasising achievement. Both are acceptable here.

exercises.question: After the surgery, he ___ (not / walk) for three months.
exercises.hint: Inability over a past period → couldn't / was not able to.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: was not able to walk / couldn't walk
Both 'couldn't' and 'was not able to' express past inability. 'Was not able to' is slightly more formal and often used in written contexts or when emphasising the difficulty.

exercises.question: Despite the noise, I ___ (eventually / sleep).
exercises.hint: Ability achieved with effort on a specific occasion → was able to (not could).
exercises.explanation:
Answer: was eventually able to sleep
For a specific single achievement that required effort on one occasion, 'was able to' (or 'managed to') is preferred over 'could'. 'Could' would suggest general ability, not a difficult specific achievement.
